19958-some-forerunners-of-italian-opera:
W. J. Henderson's Some Forerunners of Italian Opera, dated 1911, traces opera before opera. Egyptians sang jubilations to their gods, he begins. Those were florid cadences on prolonged vowel sounds. Greeks likewise caroled on vowels in honor of their deities. Such singing is older than the Christian era's foundations. Henderson builds a long runway toward Florence, where opera was born.

Henderson was the New York Sun's formidable music critic. His history honors the madrigalists and early experimenters. Monody, the sung speech of 1600, is his destination. Forerunners matter because opera claims a sudden birth. Henderson proves a long gestation instead. The book remains a readable doorway into opera's prehistory.
20264-parsifal-story-and-analysis-of-wag:
H. R. Haweis wrote Parsifal, a story and analysis of Wagner's great opera. Haweis recalls walking toward the festival through Wagner's own Bayreuth grounds. Pale petals of wild roses scatter upon his path as he goes. A stream of people moves down the avenue by the Neue Schloss.

Parsifal was Wagner's last opera, a sacred tale of the Holy Grail. Haweis retells its plot and then weighs its music and meaning. He writes for newcomers who want a guide before they listen. Readers get a warm, period doorway into Wagner's most solemn work.
21472-ned-garth-or-made-prisoner-in-afri:
Ned Garth watches a strange craft off the coast at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's Ned Garth. His uncle, Lieutenant John Pack, has lost a leg and walks with a thick stick. The two had been out on an errand of mercy to an injured fisherman.

The tale carries Ned to Africa, where he is made prisoner, as the subtitle says. Kingston aims the book squarely at the horrors of the slave trade. Sea scenes, capture, and the fight against slaving fill the action. Ned's sharp young eyes, keener than his uncle's, serve him well when danger comes close.
21907-an-investigation-into-the-nature-o:
Coal dust kills slowly in Archibald Makellar's investigation of black phthisis, reprinted at Edinburgh in 1846 from a medical journal. Makellar, a fellow of the Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh, read his findings to the Medico-Chirurgical Society in July 1845. He studied the East Lothian coal miners in particular. As the disease advances, he writes, the heart grows feeble and the blood shows a dark, carbon-like mixing.

The cause, he argues, is breathed-in filth: gunpowder smoke, lamp smoke, and dust hanging in badly aired pits. His name for it, ulceration from carbon gathered in the lungs, describes black lung disease exactly. The paper is an early landmark of workplace medicine. It gave miners' suffering a cause, a course, and a doctor's sworn witness.
22834-voyage-of-h-m-s-pandora:
A forgotten manuscript drives Voyage of H.M.S. Pandora. For more than a century, the editor notes, an account written by one of the main actors in the drama sat unread in the Record Office. The Pandora's mission gives that drama its shape. The frigate sailed to Tahiti to seize the Bounty mutineers.

The narrative follows the hunt, the capture, and the disastrous wreck on the return voyage. Prisoners in irons, a sinking ship, and open-boat escapes supply grim incident, all told from inside the expedition. Few naval stories mix triumph and horror so closely. This printing rescued a firsthand record from the archive, and it remains a key source on the Bounty affair.
22965-ten-thousand-miles-with-a-dog-sled:
Hudson Stuck measures Alaska's scale in Ten Thousand Miles with a Dog Sled, his narrative of winter travel in the interior. Alaska, he warns, is not one country at all. The territory arcs across huge spans of latitude and longitude. In climate, population, resources, and daily needs, it behaves like four or five separate lands.

Stuck, an Episcopal archdeacon, traveled his vast parish by dog team, and the book records missions, villages, cold, and dogs with equal care. Few travel books cover so much hard ground so plainly. His respect for Native Alaskans and for his teams sets the tone. The narrative stands as a classic of northern travel, written from the trail rather than about it.
a-first-family-of-tasajara:
Bret Harte opens in the general store of Sidon settlement in Contra Costa, where a gust of wind shakes the wooden building and sets the straw hats swinging on their beam. Four loafers sit out the weather while talk turns to the great family of the place. Tasajara's first family rose with California itself, from camp beginnings to ranch wealth.

The novel follows that family's pride, marriages, and slow decline as the old order of Spanish grants and mining money gives way to new men. Harte writes social comedy with a Western setting: balls, lawsuits, and duels of manners among people who remember when the land was wilderness. His irony is kind and his eye for pretension exact.
a-sketch-of-the-causes-operations-and-re:
A Sketch of the Causes, Operations and Results of the San Francisco Vigilance Committee in 1856, by Stephen Palfrey Webb, gives a mayor's eyewitness account of America's most famous vigilante movement. Webb, a Harvard graduate and Salem lawyer who served as mayor of Salem, went west about 1853 and was mayor of San Francisco in 1854 and 1855. He watched the riotous mobs that followed the Gold Rush at close range.

After returning east, Webb lectured on what he had seen and expanded his notes into this sketch, dated 1874. The Committee of 1856, formed after shootings shook the city, enrolled thousands, seized accused men from jail, tried them, and hanged several, defying the state government in the name of order. Webb's paper, preserved by his family, is valued as firsthand testimony from a trained observer who stood on the ground, neither rioter nor committee man.
a-vanished-arcadia-being-some-account-of:
R. B. Cunninghame Graham recounts the Jesuit missions of Paraguay from 1607 to 1767, as his title page states. Jesuit priests gathered the Guaraní people into mission towns, called reductions, deep in South America. There they built churches, taught crafts and music, and shielded the Guaraní from slave raiders and harsh settlers.

His chapters move from Sebastian Cabot and the first expeditions through Father Montoya's great retreat down the Paraná, quarrels with bishops and governors, and the final expulsion of the Jesuits. Graham writes with sympathy for the lost mission world and with a traveler's feel for the land. The map and the records behind the text give it weight.
antony-and-cleopatra:
William Shakespeare's tragedy, in the old-spelling text of this edition, ranges between Alexandria and Rome as two worlds pull at Mark Antony. Antony, one of Rome's three rulers, lingers in Egypt with Queen Cleopatra while affairs at home decay. His wife dies, a rival grows stronger, and duty calls him back too late.

The play moves through councils, feasts, and battles on land and sea, ending at Actium and in Egypt again. Antony and Cleopatra choose love and pride over safety, and both meet grand, theatrical deaths. Shakespeare gives Cleopatra wit, rage, and splendor, and gives Rome cold ambition in young Octavius Caesar.
c-f-meyer-die-versuchung-des-pescara:
A great general stands tempted to betray his emperor and seize Italy for himself in C. F. Meyer's Die Versuchung des Pescara, given here in German. The Temptation of Pescara sets the Marquis of Pescara at a crisis of the Italian wars, courted by offers of a crown. Meyer turns the moment into a study of ambition resisted.

His prose is precise and lapidary, every sentence cut like stone. Dying of wounds and courted by temptation, Pescara becomes a Renaissance prince in a moral laboratory. Meyer, the Swiss master of the historical novella, works here at his finest. The past feels close enough to touch, and the psychology stays modern. Few novellas pack so much statecraft and soul into so few pages.
caesar-and-cleopatra:
George Bernard Shaw wrote Caesar and Cleopatra, a play in five acts set in Egypt in 48 BC, as Julius Caesar invades during Egypt's civil war. Young Queen Cleopatra hides near the Sphinx, frightened of the Romans. Caesar meets her there and treats her with amused patience. Shaw's Caesar is aging, bald under an oak wreath, and wiser than everyone around him.

Court scenes bring in King Ptolemy, his adviser Pothinus, and Caesar's blunt officer Rufio. Britannus, Caesar's British secretary, supplies comedy with his shocked respectability. Cleopatra learns statecraft, cruelty, and charm under Caesar's eye. Shaw closes the volume with explanatory notes on his characters. Readers get history rewritten as witty argument, where talk matters as much as battles and Caesar teaches a queen how power works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abdera: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Abdera names Abdera, now Bouloustra, a titular see of Rhodope province on Thrace's south coast. The place was founded about 656 years before Christ. Nothing further is recorded in the entry, which stands as a bare geographical and historical note identifying the ancient see and its modern name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-a-san:
Abraham a Sancta Clara, a Discalced Augustinian friar, preached and wrote popular devotional books. He was born at Messkirch in Baden in 1644 and died on 1 December 1709. Eighth of nine children of a prosperous serf who kept a tavern, he was baptized John Ulrich. He was schooled in his village and at Messkirch, passed through the Jesuit school at Ingolstadt, and after his father's death was adopted by his uncle, a canon of Altotting.

In 1662 he joined the Discalced Augustinians at Vienna, taking the name Abraham in his uncle's honour, with a Sancta Clara added. Ordained in 1666, he preached at Taxa near Augsburg and was recalled to Vienna. In 1677 he became imperial court preacher to Leopold I and lived through the plague year of 1679. His vivid preaching and devotional books made him a popular voice, and the entry traces his works and their later study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-ben-m:
Abraham ben Meir Aben-Ezra, also called Ibn Ezra, was a famed Spanish rabbi, Toledo-born in 1092. He died on a journey from Rome or Rodez toward home on 23 January 1167. He excelled in philosophy and astronomy, in medicine and poetry, and in linguistics and exegesis. The Wise, the Great, and the Admirable Doctor were his epithets. Driven from Toledo by vexations inflicted on the Jews, he travelled widely through Europe, Egypt, and Palestine.

His chief work, a commentary on the Sacred Books, is nearly complete except for Paralipomenon, with his Pentateuch commentary in several revisions. He held to the literal sense, shunning rabbinic allegory and cabbalistic extravagance, yet stayed faithful to Jewish tradition. His independent criticism struck some writers as near rationalism, while his other books, like the Book of the Secrets of the Law, follow cabbalistic views and reflect his unsettled travelling life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agra:
Agra is an archdiocese in British India, lying between 25 degrees 30 minutes and 32 degrees north latitude and 75 and 81 degrees east longitude. Its area is 91,843 square miles. Its population by the last census is 28,086,364. When missions were first introduced, Mohammedanism was India's predominant religion, while Hinduism was the primitive religion. Most of the population then, as now, followed it.

The Archdiocese of Agra grew out of the Tibet Mission, the first regular establishment in this part of India. Since 1703 the Sacred Congregation of Propaganda assigned the Tibet mission to the Capuchins of the Marca d'Ancona. From 1704 to 1808 some thirty bands of missionaries, of two or three to eleven or twelve men, were sent out. None were sent from 1808 to 1823, owing to Europe's unsettled state. Ludovic Micara, consecrated bishop on 13 April 1820 for the Tibet-Hindustan Mission, was prevented by circumstances from leaving Europe, where he died a cardinal archbishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexandre-rod:
Alexandre Rodrigues Ferreira was a Brazilian naturalist and explorer, born at Bahia in 1756 and dead at Lisbon in 1815. Sent to Portugal for training, he studied at the University of Coimbra. He taught natural history there, and in 1778 was called to Lisbon to work in the Ajuda Museum. For five years he catalogued its specimens and wrote learned monographs and reports, winning election to the Lisbon Academy of Sciences.

The Portuguese government charged Ferreira with a scientific expedition into the interior of Brazil, which he undertook in 1783 and spent nine years on. From Marajó Island he crossed to the mainland and followed the Amazon and its tributaries, studying native peoples, their languages and customs, and local fauna and flora. His energy and skill won him the name of the Brazilian Humboldt. From 1793 until his death he directed Lisbon's natural history cabinet and botanical garden, though most exploration records vanished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfonso-de-za: Alfonso de Zamora was a converted Spanish rabbi, baptized in 1506 and dead in 1531. He revised the Hebrew text for Cardinal Ximenes's Polyglot Bible, translated the Chaldee paraphrase in it, and added its sixth volume. He also published his Hebrew Introductions at Alcalá in 1526. His work served the great polyglot Bible project centred at Alcalá.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alvaro-de-men:
Alvaro de Mendaña de Neyra, Spanish navigator born at Saragossa in 1541, died at Santa Cruz in the Solomon Islands on 18 October 1596. About 1558 he went to Lima at his uncle Lope García de Castro's invitation, the Viceroy, who equipped a two-ship expedition under his nephew. Sailing from Callao in November 1567, they discovered several Oceanic islands within about a year and returned to Peru in 1568.

His glowing description named them the Solomon Islands, supposing Solomon drew temple gold there. Later reports of wealth prompted a colonizing expedition under Philip II's order, sailing 11 April 1595. It discovered the Marquesas, named for the Viceroy of Peru's marquis wife, later called Nukahiva by Cook in 1774. Mendaña died before the voyage's end, delegating power to his resolute wife, who led the expedition safely to Manila in February 1596.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amadia-and-ak:
Amadia and Akra name two Chaldean Rite Catholic dioceses in Kurdistan, Turkey in Asia. Amadia first existed under another title, taking its present name only after the city of Amadia's foundation. Early in the nineteenth century the territory split into three dioceses: Amadia, Zakho, and Akra, each centred on its own town.

On 10 June 1895 the Dioceses of Amadia and Akra provisionally united, the bishop residing sometimes in one town, sometimes the other, or even at Araden. The provisional union joined two small towns under one bishop, who also sometimes resided at Araden.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amra:
Amra is the name of certain ancient Irish elegies, or praise poems, written for native saints. The most famous survivor, the Amra of Columkille, reached print with a translation by O'Beirne Crowe in 1871. Later editors, including Atkinson and Whitley Stokes, worked from imperfect copies until Stokes edited the Bodleian text with a fresh translation.

Tradition says Dallan Mac Forgaill, chief poet of his day, composed the poem about 575. He wrote in thanks for Columkille saving the bards from expulsion at the assembly of Druim Cetta. Stokes and Strachan, judging by language rather than legend, place the poem in its present form near 800. Dallan also wrote an Amra on Senan and another on Conall of Ineskeel, with whom he shared a grave.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anaphora:
A word from Greek for offering or sacrifice, anaphora belongs to the liturgy of the Greek Rite. There it names the part of the service that matches the Latin Canon of the Mass. The same word also covers the offering of Eucharistic bread, the large veil that covers it, and the procession that bears the offering to the altar.

Unlike the Roman Canon, which has stayed fixed from time immemorial, Greek anaphoras are many, though in substance they reach back to apostolic times. Their present shape dates from the late fourth or early fifth century. Basil the Great and John Chrysostom then shortened a liturgy grown long and tiring. Offertory here runs as a solemn procession, with priest, deacon, acolytes, and censer bearers carrying bread and wine through the small door of the icon screen. The article stresses what this antiquity proves about the sacrificial character of the Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Skara, the most ancient diocese in Sweden, stood suffragan to Hamburg, then Lund, then Upsala from 1164 to 1530. It covered Skaraborg, Elfsborg, and Vermland, founded about 990 at Skara, capital of the Goths. It embraced all Gauthiod until about 1100, when its eastern part became Linkoping. At first missionary bishops preached wherever they pleased.

Odinkar Hvite the Elder was apparently the first bishop stationed at Skara about 990. Yet a bishop list from about 1325 names Sigurd, court bishop to King Olaf Tryggveson, as first bishop. Sigurd founded three churches in Vestergotland and baptized Olaf Skotkonung, first Christian king of Sweden, at Husaby in 1008. Thurgaut followed as first diocesan bishop, about 1012 to 1030. His nominal successor Gotskalk, a monk of Luneburg, never left his abbey. The cathedral was restored in 1312 to 1320 and painted in fresco. Bryniolph III settled the Lund frontier, and Vincent Hennings was beheaded by Christian II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancyra:
Today's Angora is the ancient Ancyra, a titular see of Galatia in Asia Minor, suffragan to Laodicea. Legend credits Midas with its founding, and about 277 before Christ it became a chief place of the Gallic conquerors of Asia Minor. Under the empire it grew into a centre of great trade. Gams gives its episcopal list, and that of a second Ancyra in Phrygia Pacatiana.

Ancyra's fame rests above all on the Monumentum Ancyranum, the official record of the Acts of Augustus, cut in marble on an ancient temple's walls. Scholars have copied and edited it several times since the sixteenth century. Its ruins still yield valuable bas-reliefs, inscriptions, and other building fragments, keeping the city rich ground for students of the ancient world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angora:
Angora is an Armenian rite diocese in Asia Minor, in Asiatic Turkey. Europeans call it Angora, the Turks Enguru, the ancient Galatian capital known as Ancyra. Midas was its founder, and Alexander marched triumphally through it. Under the Seleucid king Antiochus III, it temporarily lost its freedom. It was capital of the Galatian kings Dejotarus and Amyntas.

When Amyntas died in 25 B.C., it became Roman, flourishing under Augustus. The Byzantines let the Persians capture it in 619. Later Arabs ravaged it, then Konia Seljukids dispossessed them. Though taken by the Crusaders, it fell to Sultan Mourad in 1362. Since then it has remained Ottoman, except after the battle of 2 July 1402. The Armenian Catholic community has a bishop, 2 churches, 1 monastery, and schools for boys and girls. The Protestant Armenians have 1 church, an American Board station directed from Caesarea. The little Latin colony, drawn by the railway, is visited by Assumption Augustinians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angra:
Angra do Heroismo is the name of Angra, the Azores' episcopal see, suffragan of Lisbon. Paul III created it in 1534, and it stood vacant from 1637 to 1671. It sits on Terceira island. Besides Terceira, it covers Sao Jorge, Graciosa, Fayal, and Pico. Flores, Corvo, Sao Miguel, and Santa Maria complete the group.

Nearly all of its 262,073 people are Catholic. Its clergy and churches number 353 priests across 108 parishes, with 41 succursal or mission churches among 332 churches and chapels. Battandier's Annuaire Pontifical Catholique (1905) and Werner's Orbis Terrarum Catholicus (1890) supply these figures, which describe a diocese covering nine islands, nearly wholly Catholic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ann-lobera:
Ann of Jesus, the Venerable Ann of Jesus, was a Carmelite nun and companion of Teresa, born in 1545, died in 1621. Daughter of Diego de Lobera and Francisca de Torres, she was deaf-mute until seven. Orphaned, she lived with relatives. After vowing virginity, she took the habit in 1570. Still a novice, Teresa called her to Salamanca over the novices. She professed in 1571 and accompanied Teresa to Beas in 1575, becoming its first prioress.

Later she founded at Granada. A misunderstanding with Teresa drew rebukes. With John of the Cross's help, constitutions were confirmed. Doria punished her for appealing to the Holy See. For three years she lost communion, intercourse, and active and passive voice. After this penance she was Salamanca prioress. A movement to bring the Teresian nuns to France carried her to Paris. She remained Brussels prioress for life. Miracles followed her death, and she was declared Venerable in 1878.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antipater-of-:
Antipater of Bostra, in Arabia, was a fifth-century Greek prelate, among the foremost of the Roman Orient, flourishing about 460. He stood out as an opponent of Origen. Almost nothing is known of his life, apart from the high esteem in which contemporaries, civil and ecclesiastical, held him. The Seventh General Council's Fathers count him among authoritative ecclesiastical writers.

Only a few fragments of his long refutation of the Apology for Origen survive, in the acts of that council. Pamphilus and Eusebius of Caesarea had put that Apology together about 309. Antipater's work was seen as a masterly composition, and as late as 540 churches of the East were ordered to read it as an antidote to spreading Origenistic heresies. Against the Apollinarists he wrote a treatise, of which only brief fragments are known, plus several homilies, two of which survive whole. His memory is kept on 13 June.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-ferre:
Lisbon poet Antonio Ferreira, born in 1528 and dead of plague there in 1569, matters both for lyric verse and for drama in Portuguese letters. He studied law at Coimbra, reading classical poetry as eagerly as legal codes, and rose to judge of the Supreme Court at Lisbon, close to the court of John III. Unlike most Portuguese poets of his day, he never wrote in Spanish, keeping always to his native tongue while joining the reform of literary taste.

Like Sá de Miranda, he left old native forms behind to advance the Renaissance, the revival of classical learning and art, showing skill with the Italian eleven-syllable line. Sonnet, elegy, idyll, verse letter, and ode all came under his hand, fed by study of Italian Renaissance poets and Greek and Latin masters. His dramatic work is where his fame chiefly rests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-vieir:
Portuguese Jesuit Antonio Vieira, born at Lisbon in 1608 and dead at Bahia in 1697, combined missionary work, diplomacy, and oratory in one long career. Taken as a child to Bahia, he was schooled by the Jesuits, joined the Society in 1623, and was ordained in 1635, astonishing hearers at once with eloquence. When the Dutch besieged Bahia in 1640, his discourse for the success of Portuguese arms was called by the sceptic Raynal the most extraordinary burst of Christian eloquence.

After Portugal broke from Spain in 1640, Vieira went to Lisbon, became tutor to the Infante Dom Pedro, a court preacher, and member of the Royal Council. He worked in war and navy affairs, revived commerce, urged a national bank and a Brazilian trade company, and championed freedom for Indians and others. The entry traces a preacher who moved from pulpit to council chamber without leaving his missionary cause behind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-cam:
The Apostolic Camera was once the central board of finance for the papal government, once important in governing the States of the Church. Today it consists of the cardinal camerlengo, or chamberlain, the vice-camerlengo, an auditor, a general treasurer and seven chamber clerics. Since the States of the Church ceased to exist, papal income now comes chiefly from Peter's pence, offerings of the faithful. The Camera has lost practical importance as a finance board.

Peter's pence is handled by a special commission, and the Camera's officials hold what are in reality honorary offices. The camerlengo's chief duties fall during a vacancy of the Holy See, when he holds a share of papal authority. The vice-camerlengo, once governor of Rome charged with peace and order, still ranks first in authority during a vacancy. The entry charts an office fading from government to ceremony.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aymara:
The Aymara are a tribe of Indians living in northern Bolivia, the eastern Andes slopes, and the Peruvian districts around Lake Titicaca, save its northern tip, held by Quichua speakers. Their numbers cannot be safely given, since three centuries of mixing blur the count. They certainly run to several thousands, counting mestizos living by Indian custom. The name Aymara fits their language, which seems allied to Quichua.

They are mountaineers of the tableland, the Puna, between the eastern Cordillera and the volcanic coast chain. They farm potatoes, quinua, and maize where altitude above twelve thousand feet allows. They raise llamas, alpacas, cattle, and donkeys, and work in towns as journeymen and on the lake shore as stevedores. They live in autonomous communities called estancias, choosing officers, hilacata and alcalde, for mostly one year, and they pay a per capita tax. Their idiom first appears in print in a 1583 catechism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balthasar-bar:
Balthasar Barreira was a Portuguese Jesuit missionary born at Lisbon in 1531, who died on Angola's mission in 1612. Angola, on Africa's southwest coast, was the scene of his life's labors. He spent his whole working life on that African mission. His writings consist chiefly of Relations sent to the Society of Jesus, describing the province's political and spiritual state.

He recounted in detail the Spaniards' 1583 victory, under Paul de Morales, over an army of native people. Accounts of pagan tribes converted and native kings baptized fill much of his work. Treatises on the people's manners and customs round out his principal subjects.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-belem-do-para:
Belém do Pará is a Brazilian archdiocese, suffragan of Bahia from 1719 and metropolitan from 3 May 1906. Its city, capital of Pará on the Bay of Guajara, bears the full name Santa Maria de Nazareth do Pará and was founded in 1615. It is South America's most northerly important port, nearest North America and Europe, and the great outlet for Pará's rubber and coffee.

The city holds 100,000 people, with exports near $25,000,000 and imports near $12,000,000 yearly. Its old Carmelite convent became a seminary, its Jesuit college now houses the episcopal palace and another seminary. The Amparo Orphan Asylum ranks among the state's leading charities, and the archdiocese counts about 480,000 Catholics. Its seventy-seven parishes are served by forty-seven secular and thirteen religious priests, with twenty-one brothers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-pere:
Benedict Pereira, a Jesuit philosopher, theologian, and Bible scholar, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born near Valencia about 1535, he died at Rome in 1610 after joining the Jesuits in 1552. In Rome he taught literature, philosophy, theology, and Scripture in turn, and left eight printed works plus much manuscript.

His great work comments on Genesis in four volumes, tackling the Flood, Noah's ark, and the tower of Babel. The entry calls it a mine of learning, praised even by critical scholars of a later age. Other writings range over philosophy and the natural world, marking him as a wide-ranging Jesuit teacher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernhard-galu:
Bernhard Galura, Prince-Bishop of Brixen, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Herbolzheim in 1764, he died in 1856 after a formation broken by Joseph II's suppression of his first convent at Altbreisach. He entered the Freiburg seminary in 1783, took a doctorate in theology, and was ordained at Vienna in 1788.

Prefect of studies at Freiburg, then bishop, he guided Brixen through the Napoleonic storms and the restoration that followed. Writings on theology and church life accompanied his long episcopate, one of the longest of his age. The entry presents a steady bishop formed in an age of suppression and rebuilding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bostra:
Bostra, the Fortress, rose from a Nabataean town to metropolis of Roman Arabia under Trajan. It is not Bosor of Reuben nor Edom's Bosrah, but perhaps the Bosora taken by the Maccabees. When Cornelius Palma destroyed the Nabataean kingdom in 105 or 106, Bostra became Nova Trajana Bostra, home of the Third Cyrenaican Legion and start of the great road to the Red Sea.

Under Alexander Severus it became a Roman colony, and Ammianus called it a great city, with ruins suggesting some 80,000 people. Colonnades, arches, baths, a theatre, temples, and churches still stand. Mahomet visited it as a trade hub, Crusaders failed to take it, and an earthquake in 1151 left it ruined. Now Bosra Eski-Sham, it holds barely 1,000 people and a small Turkish garrison.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cathedra:
A cathedra is the bishop's chair or throne in his cathedral, from which he presides at solemn functions. At first it sat mid-apse, with the benches of assisting priests on either side at a lower level. The same arrangement appears in catacomb frescoes of Christ enthroned among the apostles. The earliest thrones were high-backed armchairs rounded at the top, carved from a single block of marble.

Later forms varied. Wooden chairs were used in Africa. Some Roman basilicas cut a niche for the throne in the apse wall, and Monte Cassino keeps one with a perforated seat like those in Roman baths. The article surveys these forms and their decoration, and notes the related term faldstool for the portable seat used when a bishop officiates away from his throne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cestra:
Cestra was a titular see of Asia Minor placed by Hierocles, Georgius Cyprius, and Parthey's Notitiae episcopatuum in Isauria, under Seleucia. Epiphanius, its bishop, attended Chalcedon in 451 and signed the letter to Emperor Leo in 458. Another bishop, Elpidius, backed Severus.

Lequien guessed the town stood beside the River Cestros in Pamphylia, drawing its name from that stream. The article calls this guess inadmissible: it led the Gerarchia cattolica of 1895 to identify Cestra with Ak-Sou, which is the river's name, not a city's. The site itself has not yet been identified.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christina-ale:
An entry on Christina Alexandra, Queen of Sweden, daughter of Gustavus Adolphus, born at Stockholm in December 1626. Her father died in 1632, her mother had wished for a son, and the girl was raised by nurses, then by her aunt Catherine. By her father's command she was brought up like a boy, taught by distinguished men, and she mastered languages, history, and politics while scorning dress and feminine pastimes.

At eighteen she took up government in 1644, but she prized personal independence and leaned toward the Catholic Church. On 6 June 1654 at Uppsala she gave up the throne to her cousin Charles Gustavus and set out for Rome. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cibyra:
An entry on Cibyra, a titular see in Caria, Asia Minor, founded by the Lycian district of the Solymi. Rome let it stay independent with its territory in 130, but Murena, Sulla's lieutenant, joined it to the province of Asia in 84, making it capital of the Cibyratic district.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coimbra:

The see was restored in 1088, after Christians retook the city in 1064. Later bishops include Pedro, chancellor of King Diniz. They also include Manoel de Menezes, who fell with Dom Sebastian at Kassr-el-Kaber.

Coimbra's old cathedral rose in the first half of the twelfth century, partly at Bishop Miguel's cost. It stands as a fine Romanesque monument. The newer Renaissance cathedral from 1580 draws less praise. Santa Cruz monastery, founded in 1131, once ranked among the kingdom's richest houses. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-el:
The Council of Elvira met at Elliberis near Granada early in the fourth century, and stands as the first known council in Spain. Nineteen bishops from across the peninsula attended, with twenty-six priests sitting beside them, though only bishops signed the acts. Its date stays disputed, with proposals ranging from about 300 to 324.

Eighty-one disciplinary canons cover marriage, baptism, idolatry, fasting, excommunication, cemeteries, usury, vigils, and dealings with pagans, Jews, and heretics. Canon thirty-three gives the oldest positive church rule on clerical celibacy, while canon thirty-six, barring pictures in churches, still sparks debate over image veneration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-a:

The first, an orthodox plenary synod of 314, left twenty-five disciplinary canons, a key document for the early administration of penance. Nine canons set terms for reconciling the lapsi, Christians who had lapsed under persecution.

A Semi-Arian conciliabulum of 358, under Basil of Ancyra, condemned cruder Arian blasphemies yet taught the Son similar to the Father in all things, though different in substance. In 375 Arian bishops gathered at Ancyra again and removed several bishops from office, Gregory of Nyssa among them, closing a turbulent local record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-leopold:

He served the Cisalpine Republic at Milan and Turin, sat at the Congress of Lyons, and survived imprisonment and exile in a conspiracy case.

Retiring from politics at thirty-eight, he gave himself to the fine arts. He directed the new Academy of Fine Arts at Venice until 1827, and built its museum much as it stands today. His late passion for rare engravings left a collection of over three thousand fifteenth- and sixteenth-century prints.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniele-da-vo:

Dutt Englished the Kamandakiya Nitisara in 1896 as The Elements of Polity. Kamandaka's work is ancient India's crisp handbook of statecraft for kings. It stands in the famed line of Kautilya's teaching on rule.

Choosing ministers and guarding the treasury lead the book's sharp lessons. Envoys, allies, spies, and the arts of war fill later chapters. A king learns when to wait, when to strike, and when to yield. The maxims stay brief, shrewd, and free of wasted words throughout. Dutt's clear prose gives English readers a true classic of royal rule. Students of politics still test its maxims against modern statecraft.

Honore de Balzac's Gambara, translated by Clara Bell and James Waring, is dedicated to the Marquis de Belloy, in whose Belleville retreat Balzac first imagined the figure. Gambara is a composer worthy of Hoffmann, as the dedication says: a pilgrim at Paradise's gate with ears for angels' songs but no way through. An Italian exile in Paris, he starves while perfecting an opera about Mahomet.

A rich dilettante patronizes and ruins him, while Gambara's wife Marianna sacrifices everything, even honor, to feed the household. The middle chapters analyze the opera's cantabile until Kadijah announces the Prophet to the populace. Balzac, who loved music without mastering it, writes genius and failure in one breath.

history-of-the-donner-party-a-tragedy-of:
History of the Donner Party, a Tragedy of the Sierra, by C F McGlashan of Truckee, California, reconstructs the worst disaster of the overland trail. McGlashan's preface begins inside a starving mind. The delirium before death by starvation, he writes, is full of visions of plenty. He imagines a dying emigrant at Donner Lake. The man points at a phantom palace. Warm rooms, rich food, and sparkling wine roll through the storm on a steel pathway.

The vision is a snowbound traveler's dream of the railroad age arriving too late. Behind it lies 1846, when the Donner and Reed families, snowed in above Truckee, starved through a Sierra winter while rescue parties fought through from California. McGlashan, the Truckee editor who interviewed the survivors and guarded their story for decades, assembled letters, diaries, and testimony into the standard account. He writes as a neighbor of the graves.

Children practice greetings, questions, and simple answers about daily life. The doll needs a hat, so grandmother may be asked to sew one. Such homely scenes keep new vocabulary tied to familiar things. The book shows how language primers taught through play a century ago.
little-journey-to-puerto-rico-for-interm:
Marian M. George wrote this school journey book for intermediate grades. The Plan Book Series issued it for classroom use. George opens by asking what people mean by our new possessions. Puerto Rico, Hawaii, and the Philippines had lately joined the United States.

Cuba, she notes, is not included and will be independent. Visiting in person would teach geography best, she admits. An imaginary journey offers the next best method. Puerto Rico, nearest and easternmost of the Greater Antilles, comes first. Newspapers and lawmakers filled their days with the new possessions. George promises the other islands will follow Puerto Rico later.
madame-flirt-a-romance-of-the-beggar-s-o:
Madame Flirt is a romance of 'The Beggar's Opera' by Charles E. Pearce. Stanley Paul published it at London, first in 1922. Its motto is Lucy's line: 'Why how now, Madam Flirt.' The tale opens in the Maiden Head Inn in St. Giles.

A portly man wakes his friend Lance to look at a pretty wench. The portly man is Mr. Gay — John Gay, the opera's own author. Pearce builds his story around Gay and his famous ballad opera. Highwayman Macheath's world of rogues and singers comes alive again. London's taverns, theaters, and streets of 1728 fill the scenes. It is a lively romp through theatrical history.
major-barbara:
Major Barbara is a play by Bernard Shaw, set in Lady Britomart's library. Lady Britomart Undershaft is a managing matron of fifty, in Wilton Crescent. She is well bred, outspoken, and peremptory to the last degree. Her daughter Barbara has become a major in the Salvation Army.

Barbara's father, Andrew Undershaft, makes his fortune from guns and gunpowder. Father and daughter meet as rivals for the souls of the poor. Shaw asks whether charity or power does more good — or harm. Their debate crackles with his wit and paradox. The play's ideas still provoke argument today. It is one of Shaw's warmest battles of ideas.
mr-gladstone-and-genesis-essay-5-from-sc:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote this essay against William Gladstone's attempt to reconcile Genesis with science. It is the fifth essay in his Science and Hebrew Tradition. Gladstone, in The Dawn of Creation and Worship, had committed himself to three propositions. Genesis, he claimed, creates water, air, and land populations in that order.

Gladstone further claimed that natural science had demonstrated this fourfold order as established fact. Therefore, he argued, the Pentateuch's writer must have had divine knowledge. Huxley, Darwin's famous advocate, takes the propositions apart one by one. The essay shows Victorian Britain's science-and-scripture controversy argued at the highest level, by its two most formidable debaters.
nasa-tm-19640017899-gegenschein-orbital-: Stephen J. Paddack of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this June 1964 note on the gegenschein. The gegenschein is a faint glow seen opposite the Sun in the night sky. Catalog notes tie the work to placing and scheduling an eccentric geophysical observatory in that reference frame. The hosted sample preserves only the report's title page, with no readable body text, so its figures and schedule cannot be described from the sample itself.
nasa-tm-19650010513-numerical-integratio:
Charles M Goldstein of Lewis Research Center prepared this paper for a SHARE meeting in Los Angeles on March 1, 1965. SHARE was a user group for IBM computers. His subject was numerical integration by Gaussian quadrature, a method for finding the area under a curve by sampling it at chosen points.

Goldstein explains how the chosen points and weights give an accurate answer with few samples. That economy mattered when computer time was scarce and costly. Engineers use such integrals in many design calculations. The paper shows a practical method, written for people who had to program it and trust its results.
nasa-tm-19650018017-digital-computer-sim:
L H Byrne at Goddard Space Flight Center described, in January 1965, a computer simulation of an infrared instrument called IRIS. IRIS was an interferometer spectrometer, a device that reads heat light to identify gases. Its raw output is a wiggly pattern called an interferogram. Byrne thanks R Hanel, the IRIS experimenter, in the report.

Simulating the instrument on a computer let the team study its output in advance. They could learn how the pattern relates to real spectra. They could also test ways to analyze the data. That ground work mattered, because a flown instrument cannot be adjusted once it is in orbit.
nasa-tm-19650020213-shadow-effects-on-a-:
Ralph M Sullivan at Goddard Space Flight Center studied what shadows do to a spacecraft solar array. Solar cells are wired in series and in parallel groups. A shadow falling on part of the array does more than dim that part. It can drag down the output of cells that remain in full sunlight.

Sullivan examines that effect for a series-parallel layout. Spacecraft parts cast moving shadows as a vehicle turns in orbit. Power planners need to know the worst loss, not just the average. His study helps them size an array with a safe margin, so a passing shadow never starves the spacecraft of power.
nasa-tm-19650025624-aerodynamic-testing-:
Delivered at an aerodynamic testing conference in Washington in March 1964, this paper surveys testing done with special research aircraft. Flight research is as old as flight itself, the author notes. Early work had to prove that heavier-than-air flight was even possible. Until the early 1930s, most research stayed in ground facilities, and flight testing stayed limited.

Special aircraft let engineers test shapes and simulate flight at full scale. Ground tunnels cannot copy every effect of real air and real motion. The paper explains why flight research kept its place beside tunnels and theory. It captures a testing culture that NASA inherited and expanded.
nasa-tm-19660012940-experiments-on-ion-c:
C C Swett, R Krawec, G M Prok, and H J Hettel at Lewis Research Center ran experiments on making ion cyclotron waves in a plasma. Their paper was prepared for an April 1965 physics meeting in Washington. A radio-frequency coil, shielded so its electric field stays in, drives the waves. The plasma under study was hydrogen, in a machine that ran without pause.

Power absorbed by the plasma was their main measure. The shield added capacitance, which bent the coil's field pattern in a noted way. Ion cyclotron heating was a candidate method for heating fusion plasmas. Bench results like these showed how well a shielded coil could deliver power to the gas.
nasa-tm-19670017964-pulse-train-generato:
Robert S. Lee, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, designed a timing device in this report. The device is a solid-state pulse-train generator for rocket-borne cameras. It controls shutter timing and film advance during the short flight of a sounding rocket.

Lee's main design goals were simplicity, flexibility, accuracy, and low power use. The timing cycle starts when power is applied and recycles continuously until shutoff. For experiments that should not recycle, the clock can be clamped. Binary logic can also be added to get any chosen number of cycles.
nasa-tm-19680013256-analysis-of-fan-turb:
Warner L. Stewart and Arthur J. Glassman, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, study jet engine turbine choices in May 1968. Their subject is the fan-drive turbine of a turbofan engine. They ask how efficiency depends on the turbine's size and on how many stages it has.

The study treats the geometry in general terms first, using specific speed and specific diameter. It then works a chosen set of real turbofan conditions. Results show efficiency and diameter varying with stage count across a range of fan speeds. Engine thrust and fuel use are also tracked against turbine efficiency. Designers could read off the price of each added stage.
nasa-tm-19680018334-nasa-research-on-pro:
Jack D. Brewer surveys NASA research on vertical and short takeoff and landing aircraft in this presentation. V/STOL aircraft can rise nearly straight up, then fly forward like normal planes. NASA's Office of Advanced Research and Technology ran the program across several centers.

Flight and wind tunnel studies ran at Ames in California and Langley in Virginia. Engine component research centered at Lewis in Cleveland. Many concepts had been tested over fifteen years, Brewer notes. Most still contributed design knowledge even when they were dropped. A few, like the tilt-wing, reached prototype military versions. Except for the helicopter, no vertical takeoff aircraft had yet entered service.
nasa-tm-19680020298-the-polar-upper-atmo:
Kaichi Maeda and George Ishikawa wrote this May 1968 Goddard preprint, numbered X-641-68-198, on the polar upper atmosphere and the aurora. High above the poles, the thin upper air behaves in ways that still puzzled scientists in 1968. Winter anomalies, glowing auroras, and shining night clouds all fall within the survey's reach.

Early chapters treat winter anomalies in separate layers of the upper air, weighing weather effects against falling charged particles. A long section then covers auroras, their changes over time and place, their link to magnetic storms, and even their faint sounds. The closing chapters describe noctilucent clouds, the highest clouds known, and weigh ideas about how they form.
nasa-tm-19690020636-a-compilation-of-cur:
Alfred C. Mascy of NASA Headquarters' Mission Analysis Division compiles computer programs for low-thrust trajectory analysis in this report. Low-thrust engines push gently for months, so their trajectories need special computation. Mascy contacted all known sources and sent questionnaires to code holders.

The catalogue holds fifty-nine program descriptions in total. The codes generate flyby and rendezvous trajectories with their associated mass computations. Some handle variable thrust, while others cover constant thrust with coast arcs. An index of programs helps readers find the right code. Mascy makes no attempt to evaluate the programs against each other. The compilation simply maps what tools existed for mission designers at the time.
nasa-tm-19700005660-an-analytic-monte-ca:
P. Argentiero of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in November 1969 on a faster way to run Monte Carlo studies. Monte Carlo work uses random sampling to map how uncertain inputs spread into uncertain results. His setting is flight planning, where full simulations can cost too much computer time.

Argentiero fits a many-variable polynomial to results from the main simulation, then draws the random samples from that fit instead. The shortcut sharply cuts computer time and ranks which inputs sway the output most. He tests it on a planned Venus orbiter mission for 1972. Down-track and radial injection errors, he finds, drove the size of the midcourse fix most.
nasa-tm-19710008933-terrain-photography-:
Paul D Lowman Jr of the Goddard Space Flight Center and Herbert A Tiedemann of the Manned Spacecraft Center wrote this final geologic report in January 1971. It sums up the Synoptic Terrain Photography Experiment, flown on several Gemini missions in 1965 and 1966. Astronauts photographed the Earth to support geology, geography, and ocean study.

Crews used hand held cameras with three lens lengths and returned about eleven hundred usable color photos. The pictures covered land between thirty two degrees north and south latitude. One early result was finding an unmapped young volcanic field in northern Mexico. The report reviews the goals, gear, and main geologic findings from the full photo set.
nasa-tm-19710026040-geological-use-of-ea:
Paul D. Lowman Jr. of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in August 1971, numbered X-644-71-359, on geological uses of photographs taken from orbit. It was an invited paper for an international astronautics congress held in Brussels. Lowman argues that orbital photography is a genuinely new tool for geologists, not just aerial photography from higher up.

Four case histories make the point: unmapped faults found in southern California, and an unmapped volcanic field in northern Mexico. A third case showed the supposed Texas lineament is really a broad zone of folding and dip-slip faulting. A fourth showed how strongly wind erosion sculpts the land in North Africa. Lowman lists advantages including huge area per picture, coverage of inaccessible regions, and economical color coverage, plus uses like checking existing geologic maps.
nasa-tm-19720018210-gsfc-orbit-computati:
GSFC Orbit Computations for ISAGEX Operations reports on a worldwide geodesy campaign proposed by the French space agency in 1969. ISAGEX, the International Satellite Geodesy Experiment, gathered precise laser and camera observations of satellites. The goal was a uniform, well-spread measurement set for studying Earth's shape, gravity, and motion.

Data gathering ran from December 1970 through August 1971 in seven three-week saturation tracking periods. Seven geodetic satellites were tracked, including GEOS-1, GEOS-2, and the French PEOLE. This report describes how Goddard's Geodynamics Branch generated acquisition data for its two laser stations during the campaign. Quick-look laser data used in a multi-arc adjustment fixed the Guam station's coordinates to within about fifteen meters in Earth's center-of-mass frame.
nedra:
George Barr McCutcheon published Nedra in 1906, with pictures by Harrison Fisher. McCutcheon had already found fame with Beverly of Graustark and Brewster's Millions. Chapter heads open with The Inspiration, The Beginning of Flight, and The First Obstacle.

Mr and Miss Ridge sail for Manila, and Mr Ridge meets glum days and a beautiful stranger. A wreck sinks the Tempest Queen, and the tale shifts to a wonderful land. There the castaways are hailed as gods from the sea, and a place called Nedra gives the book its name. An enemy then nears, and battle looms. Romance and shipwreck drive the plot.
old-fritz-and-the-new-era:
Luise Mühlbach wrote this historical novel about Frederick the Great. Peter Langley translated it from the German. The Germans called the old king Old Fritz. Book one shows the lonely king and court life. Chapters name parades, oaths, and a drive to Berlin.

Book two turns to Rosicrucians and men of claimed power. Goethe appears in Berlin and visits the court world. Love, hate, and secret groups drive the plot onward. Mühlbach was a popular novelist of Prussian history. Book one also names Wilhelmine Enke and a gold rain tale. Book two adds a Jesuit chief and the king's own letter.
outlines-of-the-earth-s-history-a-popula:
Nathaniel Southgate Shaler was Harvard's professor of geology. He wrote Outlines of the Earth's History as a popular study in physiography. That is the science of the earth's surface and its making. His preface states the object plainly. Beginners should grasp the actions of nature that anyone can follow. Those processes made this world and other spheres too.

Textbooks, Shaler complains, present the earth's story as finished. That feeds the idea that the universe is done, not endlessly doing. He chose facts that show energy at work without pause. The reader should gain science's largest impression: events in swift, unending procession. The frontispiece teaches it in one image. Dunes at Ipswich Light show bushes arresting wind-blown sand.
pandora:
Henry James's novella Pandora opens aboard a North German Lloyd steamer. The Donau has anchored for hours at Southampton. American passengers stream across the plank to join the Bremen sailing. A young German diplomat watches them from the bulwarks. Count Otto Vogelstein smokes and judges, comfortably nested already. He wonders whether to condemn the custom or approve it.

Vogelstein is bound for Washington. He has been appointed secretary of the German legation there. James describes him with amused precision: serious, civil, ceremonious, curious, stiff. His spectacles gleam; his moustache curves discreetly. He is stuffed with knowledge and proud of the German Empire. Yet he inquires with eyes, ears, and nose as much as tongue. America, his vast field of study, is about to board his ship.
podcast-joerogan-psEcI7s2MRA:
Jordan Peterson takes on unearned moral superiority in this clip drawn from Joe Rogan Experience episode 877. Peterson argues that many people claim virtue without paying any real cost for it. The short segment pulls one sharp theme from a much longer talk.

Peterson says performing goodness online is easier than living well in private. He urges people to fix their own lives before lecturing the world. Rogan nods along and adds examples from public life and social media shaming. The clip distills Peterson's core message: real morality shows in action, not in posture.
podcast-tuckercarlson-0j1gcGD5DrA:
Billionaire investor Ray Dalio joins Tucker Carlson to warn of America's hidden civil war and its race with China. Dalio, founder of Bridgewater, studies history in big cycles of rise and decline. His forecast here is sober, from a man who has called major turns before.

Dalio explains the signs he sees of internal conflict and weakening order in the United States. He compares America's position with China's in tech, economics, and universities. Carlson asks what citizens and investors should do with such a warning. Serious and investor-minded viewers get a big-cycle briefing on the country's road ahead.
queen-hortense-a-life-picture-of-the-nap: Queen Hortense, a life picture of the Napoleonic era by L. Mühlbach, translated from the German by Chapman Coleman and dated 1910, is shown here by its title page and contents. Book one, Days of Childhood and of the Revolution, runs through General Bonaparte, the marriage, Italy, and the return from Egypt. Book two, The Queen of Holland, covers Louis Bonaparte, consul and king, calumny, Napoleon's heir, and the divorce.
schwatka-s-search-sledging-in-the-arctic:
William H. Gilder served as second in command on Lieutenant Schwatka's Arctic sledging trip and wrote the expedition's story in Schwatka's Search. The party went north hunting for records of the lost Franklin expedition. A portrait of Schwatka faces the title page, and a long introduction sets out what the journey settled.

Quoting an English newspaper of September 25, 1880, the introduction credits Schwatka with ending doubt about how Franklin's men died. His party found where the missing ship lay, cleared the local people of blame, and guarded the crew's graves from animals. One body came home for burial, markers rose over the rest, and gathered objects let families know their dead. Gilder also explains that much of the story first appeared as his letters to the New York Herald.
stories-of-the-wagner-opera:
H. A. Guerber wrote Stories of the Wagner Opera. She had already written Myths of Greece and Rome and Myths of Northern Lands. Dodd, Mead and Company printed the book at New York in 1905. The copyright dates to 1895. A portrait of Richard Wagner stands at the front.

Guerber's preface says each sketch can be read in a few minutes. The sketches aim to give a clear outline of the great composer-dramatist's work. Verse quotations are woven through the text. The contents begin with Rienzi, the Last of the Tribunes, and The Flying Dutchman. The book serves listeners who want the plots and spirit of the operas in short, plain form before or after a performance.
studies-in-song-a-century-of-roundels-so:
Volume V of the Collected Poetical Works of Algernon Charles Swinburne carries the heading Studies in Song: A Century of Roundels: Sonnets on English Dramatic Poets: The Heptalogia. The pages at hand show the volume's opening run of shorter poems before the named sets begin.

Their titles sketch Swinburne's range: Athens: An Ode, The Statue of Victor Hugo, Euthanatos, lines on the death of Edward John Trelawny, and a farewell piece in French, Adieux a Marie Stuart. A group of child poems follows: A Child's Pity, A Child's Laughter, A Child's Thanks, A Child's Battles, and A Child's Future. Roundels, a form he made his own, give the volume its playful music.
tanakh-jps-1917-ezra:
Ezra is a history book of the Hebrew Bible, presented in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society version of the Holy Scriptures. It opens in the first year of Cyrus, king of Persia, at the end of exile in Babylon.

Cyrus makes a decree through all his realm that Jews may go up to Jerusalem and rebuild God's house. He urges each town to aid those who go with silver, gold, goods, and beasts. Chiefs of Judah and Benjamin, priests, and Levites then rise to make the trip, and Cyrus brings out the temple vessels once seized. Readers follow a return built on a king's grant, shared gifts, and hope for a restored house of worship.
taquisara:
F. Marion Crawford published his novel Taquisara in 1895, set amid the high society of Naples and Rome. It opens in a library, where a young princess must sign a formal paper under the eye of a notary.

Veronica Serra holds an old silver pen with thin, dark fingers and feels a sharp dislike for Lamberto Squarci, the smooth notary beside her. A blot of ink falls before she can write, and his calm repair of the spot does not ease her dread. Readers enter a tale of rank, money, and marriage, where a forced signature hints at plots laid around an heiress.
the-beggar-s-opera:
A 1922 Heinemann edition follows a 1765 text and opens with a talk between a Beggar and a Player. The Beggar claims poverty as his title to poetry and says he belongs to the company of beggars at St Giles. He has a small yearly salary for his catches and a welcome at their dinners.

He explains that the piece was written for the marriage of two ballad singers, James Chaunter and Moll Lay. It borrows the similes of grand opera, he says, and adds a prison scene that ladies find moving. With no recitative, prologue, or epilogue, he still claims it is an opera in all its forms.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-15-ezr:
Ezra in the authorised King James wording, opens in the first year of Cyrus, king of Persia, when a word spoken by Jeremiah is fulfilled. God stirs Cyrus's spirit, and the king makes a proclamation through his kingdom and puts it in writing.

Cyrus declares that the God of heaven has given him all kingdoms and charged him to build a house at Jerusalem. Any of God's people may go up and build, helped by neighbours with silver, gold, goods, and beasts. Freewill offerings are also named. Return from exile starts not with escape, but with a royal licence and public support.
the-duenna-a-comic-opera:
The Duenna, a comic opera first played at Covent Garden on November 21, 1775, opens with its cast as first acted. Don Ferdinand, Don Jerome, Don Antonio, and Don Carlos lead the men; Donna Louisa and Donna Clara lead the women, with Mrs. Green as the Duenna. The scene is Seville, and Lopez speaks first, past three in the morning.

Lopez, lantern in hand, grumbles that serving a young lover is the hardest post of all. Songs, disguise, and a scheming duenna drive Richard Brinsley Sheridan's farce of love and gold. Elopements and errors pile up fast.
the-fables-of-aesop-selected-told-anew-a:
Joseph Jacobs picked and retold these fables of Aesop, and traced their history, in a London book of 1894 with pictures by Richard Heighway. A short history of the Aesopic fable comes before the tales.

Familiar beast tales fill the contents. They run from the Cock and the Pearl and the Wolf and the Lamb to the Fox and the Crow. The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse stand among them. So does the Lion and the Mouse. Each short tale ends in a plain moral about greed, pride, or kindness. Jacobs gives readers both the stories and an account of how they traveled down the ages.
the-history-of-sumatra: William Marsden, F.R.S., wrote The History of Sumatra. The record shows a third edition, printed in London in 1811. The edition carries corrections, additions, and plates. The title page promises a wide account of the island. It covers government, laws, customs, and manners. It also covers the natural productions of Sumatra. The ancient political state of the island is included. A plate of a Malay boy of Bencoolen is noted. Only the title page and contents heading are present here.
the-lion-of-petra:
Talbot Mundy opens his Arabian adventure by denying that it tells of any animal. No four legged lions live at Petra now, the narrator says, and the real lion there is a man. Assyrian kings once hunted near Petra and carved boasts about their kills.

Chapter titles in Arab proverb style promise Ali Higg, a black tent, kites, and twenty aeroplanes. The narrator Grim and his partner meet their lion in the year 1920. Mundy mixes desert politics, hidden wealth, and a scheming holy man in country ruled by rumor and rifles after the Great War.
the-lost-ambassador-or-the-search-for-th: E. Phillips Oppenheim's The Lost Ambassador, or The Search for the Missing Delora, was published in Boston by Little, Brown, and Company in 1910, with illustrations in color by Howard Chandler Christy. Only the title page and part of the contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. The chapters shown match the companion record of the same book: A Rencontre, A Café in Paris, Delora, Dangerous Play, and Delora Disappears among them. Oppenheim's other works named here include The Illustrious Prince and Jeanne of the Marshes.
the-march-of-portola-and-the-discovery-o: Zoeth S. Eldredge wrote The March of Portolá and the Discovery of the Bay of San Francisco. The Reception Committee of the California Promotion Committee published it, with the endorsement of the Portolá Festival's committee. It pairs his narrative with the log of the San Carlos and original documents, translated and annotated by E. J. Molera. Only the title pages, an epigraph poem, and contents are present, so the narrative itself does not appear. The contents promise an introduction, data on Portolá's later years, and a viceroy's letter.
the-mysterious-shin-shira:
G. E. Farrow's children's book The Mysterious Shin Shira, illustrated by W. G. Easton and published in London by Henry Frowde with Hodder and Stoughton, is present here only in title page and contents, so the mysteries themselves do not appear. A frontispiece promises a terrible dragon lying a short distance beyond, with a reference to page 28. Farrow is billed as author of The Wallypug of Why.

Contents divide the book into numbered mysteries with page numbers. Shin Shira Appears opens at page 9, Shin Shira and the Dragon at page 23, and The Magic Carpet at page 33. Shin Shira and the Duchess, the Lame Duck, and the Diamond follow before the list breaks off at Mystery No. VII.
the-narrative-of-lunsford-lane-formerly-:
The Narrative of Lunsford Lane, formerly of Raleigh, North Carolina, was published by Lane himself at Boston in 1842, printed by J. G. Torrey. Its full title promises an account of his early life. It also promises the redemption by purchase of himself and his family from slavery. His banishment from his birthplace, for the crime of wearing a coloured skin, completes the promise. A transcriber's note warns that the text came from a contemporary printing, not the 1842 edition, so some spellings may be modernised.

Before the narrative proper stands an original poem, The Slave Mother's Address to Her Infant Child. The mother tells her baby she cannot say how much she loves to look on him. Her soul rocks as on a tempest. She knows despair's curtains will soon close around a child born into slavery.
the-phantom-of-the-opera: Gaston Leroux wrote The Phantom of the Opera, listed here with a 1909 date. The front matter and part of the contents are all that is present, so the novel itself does not appear. Leroux is billed as author of The Mystery of the Yellow Room. Chapters shown run from a prologue and Is It A Ghost? through The New Margarita, Box Five, The Enchanted Violin, and At the Masked Ball, breaking off at chapter ten in the list present.
the-strand-magazine-vol-07-issue-37-janu: The Strand Magazine, an illustrated monthly edited by George Newnes, opens its seventh volume with the January 1894 issue. Only the title page and contents appear here. They promise pieces. Stories from a doctor's diary lead off. The Queen of Holland and zoo zig-zags follow. A helmet story from the French comes next. The music of nature and portraits of celebrities, Sir Henry Loch among them, appear too. Reminiscences of Sir Andrew Clark follow. J. Holt Schooling writes on the signatures of Charles Dickens. The articles themselves do not appear.
the-vicomte-de-bragelonne-the-end-and-be:
John Bursey writes about Dumas's Vicomte de Bragelonne rather than retelling it, in an essay subtitled The End and Beginning of an Era. Earlier D'Artagnan romances, he says, unite four heroes against clear villains with swordplay, bravado, and luck. Their cry of all for one echoes after a hundred fifty years, through films, adverts, and even a candy bar.

The final volume differs because the heroes are no longer united. Aramis plots against the king, dragging Porthos along, while D'Artagnan has sworn to defend that king with his life. Athos must break his sword before his monarch. Bursey also defends Dumas against charges of running a literature factory, crediting collaborator Maquet with research and Dumas with the drama's life.
the-wagner-story-book-firelight-tales-of: William Henry Frost retells Wagner's music dramas as fireside stories in The Wagner Story Book, illustrated by Sydney Richmond Burleigh. The volume is dedicated to Helen Krebbier. The pages present here give the title, contents, and illustrations list, so the tales themselves do not appear. Eleven story titles map onto the operas. The Stolen Treasure, The Daughter of the God, The Hero Who Knew No Fear, and The End of the Ring cover the Ring cycle. The Knight of the Swan and The Love Potion follow.
the-waters-of-edera:
Ouida, author of Moths and Under Two Flags, published The Waters of Edera with T. Fisher Unwin in London in 1900. Her opening chapter surveys a lonely country of wide pastures, heather moors, rock-born streams, and forests, with the sea eastward unseen and mountains always changing in aspect. Minerals sleep unsought under the turf, and temple ruins wear wild berries.

Buffalo browse where emperors feasted, and bitterns cross forgotten battlefields. Then the flocks come through, driven along the Edera water from plains to hills. Goatskin-clad shepherds look like savage satyrs, and lambs that cannot keep pace have their throats slit for the evening fire. Ouida's pastoral beauty carries a hard, unsentimental edge from the first pages.
the-world-english-bible-web-ezra:
Ezra, book fifteen of the World English Bible, begins with a Persian king's decree. Cyrus rules in his first year when God stirs his spirit. The decree fulfills Jeremiah's prophecy about exile ending. Cyrus proclaims that God gave him all earthly kingdoms. He is charged to build God's house in Jerusalem. Any of God's people may return and rebuild it.

Neighbors must help the travelers with silver, gold, and animals. Freewill offerings support the temple work. Exile thus ends by royal proclamation. Rebuilding worship in a ruined city drives the book. Readers see a small community restart under imperial permission.
trees-fruits-and-flowers-of-minnesota-19: Trees, Fruits and Flowers of Minnesota for 1916 forms volume forty-four of the Minnesota State Horticultural Society's publications. It embraces the society's transactions from December 1, 1915 to December 1, 1916, plus twelve numbers of The Minnesota Horticulturist. Secretary A. W. Latham edited the volume at Minneapolis. A frontispiece shows a ten-foot monument built from twenty-five bushels of apples at the society's annual meeting. Only the title pages and opening notices are present here, so the year's papers themselves do not appear.
voyages-of-peter-esprit-radisson-being-a:
Peter Esprit Radisson's Voyages, printed for the Prince Society, tell his travels among the North American Indians from 1652 to 1684. The text was copied from his own manuscripts, kept in the Bodleian Library and the British Museum, and Gideon D. Scull supplied historical notes and an introduction. The preface counts it luck that the society could add the book to its publications at all.

Radisson, the preface says, was a chief actor in the events he records, and wrote with no thought of print. His journals slept in manuscript for more than two hundred years, missed even by scholars, with no extracts in print. He was a Frenchman with an imperfect grasp of English, which the editors let stand. Readers get a fur trader's and explorer's own account of the Canadian woods, canoes, councils, and wars of the first French years.
walsh-report-vol-1-iran-contra:
Lawrence E. Walsh, a former federal judge, served as Independent Counsel for the Iran-Contra affair from 1986 to 1993. This first volume of his final report, dated August 4, 1993, covers the investigations and prosecutions. The report is a United States government work, open to the public.

Walsh lays out the arms-for-hostages deals with Iran and the diversion of profits to Nicaragua's Contras, against a legal ban. He then follows his cases against Oliver North, John Poindexter, Robert McFarlane, Richard Secord, and others. Convictions won and lost, pardons granted by President Bush, and evidence withheld all enter the record. It is the scandal's official autopsy.
zenobia-or-the-fall-of-palmyra:
William Ware wrote this historical novel as a series of letters from Palmyra. Letter one comes from Piso, a Roman lately of the Coelian hill. He writes to his friend Curtius back in Rome. Everything around him feels dreamlike in its strangeness, he says. Splendour surrounds him, yet he longs for home. His errand in the East has brought sorrow as well as wonder.

Piso recalls losing sight of Curtius weeping on the quay. The Tiber's crowds, galleys, and wild beast cargoes then filled his departure. Aurelian and Queen Zenobia's city stand behind the letters. Readers get Rome's eastern war through a homesick witness.
